::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a driving test with a fixed route"}
You can't judge a driver from one trip they chose themselves. A driving test uses a fixed route, with known hard spots, the same for everyone; the examiner ticks a checklist, and some boxes are exact ("stopped at the line") while others need judgement ("drove smoothly"). And examiners are themselves checked: a second examiner sometimes rides along, to see whether they agree.

An **evaluation** is that test for Atlas: fixed questions with known answers, exact checks wherever possible, a judge for what can't be checked exactly, and a check on the judge.
:::

## The problem

Lesson 6.7 ended with an answer that looked good, cited real lines, and was half wrong. Every change to Atlas (a new prompt, more sources, another embedding model, a different chunk size) might make answers better or worse, and trying three questions by hand tells you almost nothing: you remember the impressive answers and forget the bad ones, and the model gives a different answer each time anyway.

What Atlas needs is a number per quality that matters, measured the same way every time, on enough questions that one lucky or unlucky answer doesn't decide it, and checked automatically on every pull request, so a change that makes Atlas worse can't be merged without someone deciding that's acceptable.

## Theory

### An evaluation set

An **evaluation set** is a fixed list of **cases**: inputs with something known about the right output. Atlas's cases are questions about Ignite, each with the files a good answer must come from:

```json
{"id": "nan-loss", "question": "How do I stop training if the loss becomes NaN?", "expected_paths": ["ignite/handlers/terminate_on_nan.py"]}
{"id": "coreml", "question": "How do I export a model to Core ML for iPhones?", "expected_paths": []}
```

Expected files, not expected answers: an answer can be worded a hundred ways, but if it's right, it cites `terminate_on_nan.py`. A case with no expected files is one Atlas should **decline**, because Ignite doesn't contain the answer. Both kinds matter: a system that never declines looks great on answerable questions.

Each expected file was checked by reading Ignite at commit `0abbcab`, and the set pins that commit: when files move, cases can silently stop meaning what they say.

### Retrieval metrics

Retrieval comes first because it is the ceiling (lesson 6.7): if search doesn't find the file, no model can cite it. For each answerable case, take the **rank** of the first result from an expected file (1 if it's the top result, none if it's not in the top 10). Then:

- **recall@k** is the share of cases whose rank is at most k. recall@5 = 0.6 means "for 60% of the questions, a right file was in the top five".
- **Mean reciprocal rank** (MRR) is the average of 1/rank, counting 0 when not found. It rewards finding things *early*: rank 1 counts fully, rank 2 half, rank 7 a seventh.

Worked example, the one in the tests: four questions found at ranks 1, 2, 7 and never.

| | rank 1 | rank 2 | rank 7 | not found | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| in top 5? | yes | yes | no | no | recall@5 = 2/4 = 0.5 |
| in top 10? | yes | yes | yes | no | recall@10 = 3/4 = 0.75 |
| 1/rank | 1 | 0.5 | 0.143 | 0 | MRR = 1.643/4 = 0.411 |

Retrieval metrics are **exact**: no model, no judgement, the same number every run (given the same index), and they take seconds.

### Checking answers exactly

Some things about an answer are exact too:

- **Cites an expected file**: did any `[n]` point at one of the case's files?
- **Valid citations**: does every `[n]` match a source (lesson 6.7)?
- **Wrongly refused**: did Atlas decline an answerable question?
- **Correctly refused**: did it decline an unanswerable one?

None of these say whether the answer is *true*. An answer can cite the right file and misread it, which is exactly what lesson 6.7's `every` answer did.

### A model as judge

Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the lines it cites is a question only a reader can answer. Reading every answer by hand doesn't scale to every pull request, so a common approach is **LLM-as-judge**: give a model the sources and the answer, and ask for a structured verdict (lesson 6.3):

```python
class Verdict(BaseModel):
    supported: bool
    unsupported_claims: list[str]
```

The catch is that the judge is a model, with all the failure modes of the model it judges. So the judge is evaluated too: a person grades a fixed set of answers by hand, and the judge's verdicts on *the same answers* are compared with theirs. The **agreement rate** is how far the judge can be trusted. A judge that hasn't been checked this way is a random number generator with good manners.

### Regression checks

A **regression** is something that used to work and no longer does. A **regression check** runs the evaluation on every change and fails if a score drops below a **threshold**, the lowest acceptable value. Thresholds come from measured scores, minus a margin for run-to-run variation (the chat model doesn't give the same answer twice), and only for metrics that can be trusted.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    C[evals/ignite.jsonl<br/>30 cases] --> R[Retrieval<br/>rank of first expected file]
    R --> RM[recall@5, recall@10, MRR<br/>per search mode]
    C --> A[Answer each question<br/>as POST /ask would]
    A --> X[Exact checks<br/>expected file, valid citations,<br/>refusals]
    A --> J[Judge model<br/>every claim supported?]
    H[evals/hand_grades.jsonl<br/>10 answers graded by a person] --> JA[Judge agreement]
    J -.checked by.-> JA
    RM --> T{evals/thresholds.json}
    X --> T
    T -->|below| F[CI fails]
    T -->|at or above| P[CI passes]
```

## In the project

### Red: the arithmetic and the gate

```python
def test_recall_and_mean_reciprocal_rank() -> None:
    # Found first, found second, found seventh, never found.
    scores = retrieval_scores([1, 2, 7, None])

    assert scores == {
        "recall_at_5": 0.5,  # two of four in the top 5
        "recall_at_10": 0.75,
        "mrr": round((1 + 1 / 2 + 1 / 7) / 4, 3),
    }


def test_scores_below_a_threshold_are_reported_and_unmeasured_ones_skipped() -> None:
    scores = {
        "retrieval": {"hybrid": {"recall_at_5": 0.6}},
        "answers": {"cites_expected": 0.9, "wrongly_refused": 0.2},
    }
    thresholds = {
        "retrieval.hybrid.recall_at_5": 0.7,
        "answers.cites_expected": 0.8,
        "answers.wrongly_refused": 0.1,  # lower is better
        "answers.supported": 0.5,  # not in this run
    }

    problems = evals.below_thresholds(scores, thresholds)

    assert problems == [
        "retrieval.hybrid.recall_at_5 is 0.6, below the threshold of 0.7",
        "answers.wrongly_refused is 0.2, above the threshold of 0.1",
    ]
```

And a whole run against the sample repository, with the fake embedder and a fake model playing both answerer and judge: one answerable case ("def accuracy return") and one to decline ("bake bread"). It checks every score, and that "bake bread" never reached the model (`len(ollama.requests) == 2`: one answer, one verdict). A last test reads the committed cases and checks their ids are unique and that both kinds exist.

### Green: `atlas/evals.py`

The rank and the scores:

```python
def first_relevant_rank(paths: list[str], expected: list[str]) -> int | None:
    """The position (from 1) of the first result from an expected file, if any."""
    for position, path in enumerate(paths, start=1):
        if path in expected:
            return position
    return None


def retrieval_scores(ranks: list[int | None]) -> dict[str, float]:
    count = len(ranks)
    found_in_5 = sum(1 for rank in ranks if rank is not None and rank <= 5)
    found_in_10 = sum(1 for rank in ranks if rank is not None and rank <= 10)
    reciprocal = sum(1 / rank for rank in ranks if rank is not None)
    return {
        "recall_at_5": round(found_in_5 / count, 3),
        "recall_at_10": round(found_in_10 / count, 3),
        "mrr": round(reciprocal / count, 3),
    }
```

Answering a case reuses lesson 6.7's functions, so the evaluation measures exactly what `POST /ask` does:

```python
def answer_case(session, chat, repo, case, query_vector, model) -> AnswerOutcome:
    """Answer one question as POST /ask would, then check the answer."""
    started = time.monotonic()
    sources = answer.find_sources(session, repo, case.question, query_vector, model)
    text = answer.NOT_FOUND
    if sources:
        text = chat.complete(answer.answer_request(case.question, sources, history=[])).text
    seconds = time.monotonic() - started

    refused = answer.NOT_FOUND.rstrip(".") in text
    cited, invalid = answer.check_citations(text, sources)
    cited_paths = [source.path for source in cited]
    cites_expected = any(path in case.expected_paths for path in cited_paths)

    # Only answers that make claims are judged: a refusal has nothing to support.
    verdict = None
    should_judge = case.answerable and not refused and bool(cited)
    if should_judge:
        verdict = judge_answer(chat, cited, text)
    return AnswerOutcome(...)
```

(Type hints trimmed.) `judge_answer` sends the cited sources and the answer with the `Verdict` schema, and returns `None` if the reply isn't a valid verdict, which counts as "not judged" rather than as either answer. `judge_agreement` re-judges the answers in `evals/hand_grades.jsonl`, which stores each graded answer *with the exact sources it cited*, so the judge sees what the person saw. And `below_thresholds` compares scores with `evals/thresholds.json`, where names like `"retrieval.hybrid.recall_at_5"` are paths into the report.

`atlas eval` runs it all and prints a summary; `--retrieval-only` skips the chat model and takes seconds, `--report` writes every case's result as JSON, and `--thresholds` makes the exit code 1 when a score is below its threshold.

### In CI: `.github/workflows/evals.yml`

A separate workflow, so it doesn't slow down the fast checks. On every pull request that touches `atlas/` or `evals/`, it starts Postgres and Ollama, pulls both models (cached between runs: 1.4 GB), fetches Ignite at the pinned commit, runs `atlas index` and `atlas embed`, then `atlas eval` with the thresholds and hand grades, and uploads the report as an artifact even when the evaluation fails, so the failing cases can be read. It takes about an hour, almost all of it embedding Ignite on the runner's CPU.

FIRST_CI_RUN

## What the measurements found

### Retrieval

```text
retrieval keyword  recall_at_5 0.2, recall_at_10 0.24, mrr 0.186
retrieval semantic recall_at_5 0.56, recall_at_10 0.64, mrr 0.403
retrieval hybrid   recall_at_5 0.64, recall_at_10 0.72, mrr 0.442
```

The same story as lesson 6.6's ten questions, on twenty-five: hybrid search beats either alone. It also sets the ceiling: for 36% of the questions, no expected file reaches the five sources the model reads.

### The similarity gate

Lesson 6.7 set the similarity threshold at 0.6 from two questions. Here is the nearest chunk's similarity for all thirty:

```text
0.548  UNANSWERABLE capital
0.554  UNANSWERABLE weather
0.587  UNANSWERABLE bread
0.624  answerable   time-limit
0.653  UNANSWERABLE kubernetes
0.654  answerable   change-lr
0.654  UNANSWERABLE coreml
0.655  answerable   every-n
0.690  answerable   save-every-epochs
...
0.811  answerable   supervised-trainer
```

No threshold separates the two kinds. Everyday questions sit below 0.6; but "How do I write a Kubernetes deployment manifest?" (0.653) and "How do I export a model to Core ML?" (0.654) sound like the codebase and score above three questions it can answer. Raising the threshold to 0.66 would block them, and three answerable questions with them. 0.6 stays; the technical ones have to be caught by the prompt's "couldn't find" rule. Whether they are is what `correctly_refused` measures, and the runs below show it isn't always.

### Answers: the first run

```text
30 cases in 14.9 min
answers   cites_expected 0.48, valid_citations 1.0, wrongly_refused 0.0, correctly_refused 1.0, supported 1.0, judged 25
```

Every citation pointed at a real source, every answerable question got an answer, every unanswerable one was declined. But only 12 of 25 answers cited an expected file, fewer than retrieval's 16 of 25 in the top five: given the right file among five sources, the model sometimes cited another. And the judge said every one of 25 answers was fully supported. That last number is the one to be suspicious of.

### A bug the evaluation found

Reading the answers (the report has every one) turned up this, answering "How do I combine precision and recall into one score?":

```text
... The `Rouge` class in `_pyrouge.py` [5] also uses a similar approach to compute a score based on
precision and recall.

EarlyStopping takes a patience argument [2].
```

The last sentence is the example from lesson 6.7's citation rule, copied word for word into an answer about F1 scores. A small model can treat an example as content. The rule now shows only the format (`like this: [2]`), and the runs below use it. Nobody would have found this from a handful of manual tries.

### Checking the judge

Ten answers from the first run, graded by hand against their cited sources, with a reason for each: four fully supported, six not. Two of the six:

- *How often are predictions correct?* The answer presents ROUGE's `Score.precision` (`match / candidate`) as the general measure of correct predictions. The source doesn't say that.
- *How do I smooth a metric over recent iterations?* Its claims about BLEU's smoothing functions are accurate; its conclusion, that they smooth a metric over iterations, is in no source.

The judge on the same ten answers, twice:

```text
run 1: agreed 4/10 in 13s; disagreements: [how-often-correct, running-average, save-every-epochs, f1, time-limit, confusion]
run 2: agreed 4/10 in 12s; ...the same six
```

It called every answer supported, so it agreed only on the four that were. A second design asked the judge to list each claim with the exact source words that state it, and computed the verdict in code. Same 4 of 10, twice, at 35 seconds an answer instead of 1.3. Its claims for the F1 answer show why:

```text
- supported=True  claim: The `precision` is calculated as `tp_summation / y_true_positive_count`.
    evidence: 'recall = tp_summation / y_true_positive_count'
- supported=True  claim: EarlyStopping takes a patience argument.
    evidence: 'EarlyStopping takes a patience argument'
```

The first "evidence" is the line for *recall*. The second is quoted from the answer itself, not from any source. The judge skipped the answer's real errors (the F1 formula appears in no source) and invented support for the rest.

So a 1.7-billion-parameter model can't judge grounding here. That's what checking the judge is for: without the hand grades, "supported 1.0" would have looked like excellent news. Atlas keeps the simple judge (same agreement, 25 times faster), reports its verdict and its agreement in every run, and lets **no threshold depend on it**. A stronger judge, such as a hosted model (lesson 6.2's `ClaudeChat`), would be measured against the same ten hand grades before being trusted.

### Variation and thresholds

Two more full runs, with the fixed citation rule:

```text
== run 2
30 cases in 12.9 min
retrieval hybrid   recall_at_5 0.64, recall_at_10 0.72, mrr 0.442
answers   cites_expected 0.52, valid_citations 1.0, wrongly_refused 0.0, correctly_refused 0.8, supported 1.0, judged 25
judge     agreed with the hand grades on 4 of 10
== run 3
30 cases in 6.4 min
retrieval hybrid   recall_at_5 0.64, recall_at_10 0.72, mrr 0.442
answers   cites_expected 0.56, valid_citations 1.0, wrongly_refused 0.0, correctly_refused 1.0, supported 1.0, judged 25
judge     agreed with the hand grades on 4 of 10
```

Retrieval is identical every time: no model samples anything there. `cites_expected` went 0.48, 0.52, 0.56, which looks like a trend and is noise (the exercise below shows the cases underneath). And in run 2, the Core ML question wasn't declined:

```text
To export a model to Core ML for iPhones, you can use the `torch-core-ml` library. First, ensure your
model is saved as a PyTorch checkpoint. Then, use the `coremltools` library to convert the model. ...
[2] provides guidance on logging model weights, which is useful for debugging, but the actual
conversion is handled by `coremltools`. ... [2]
```

A made-up library, cited to an unrelated example file. Run 3's "correctly_refused 1.0" hid a worse version:

```text
To export a model to Core ML for iPhones, you can use the `torch.core` module to convert the model to
the Core ML format. ... using the `torch.core.export` function. ... [1] outlines the addition of
gradient scaling ... Therefore, the answer is: I couldn't find this in the indexed code.
```

An invented function, four citations, and *then* the refusal sentence. The check counted any answer containing that sentence as a refusal, so this counted as correct. That's a bug in the evaluation, not just the model, and it's the reason to read answers rather than only scores. A refusal now has to say so *and cite nothing*:

```python
# A refusal says so and cites nothing. A small model sometimes writes a made-up answer
# with citations and then adds "I couldn't find this..."; that isn't declining (6.8).
says_not_found = answer.NOT_FOUND.rstrip(".") in text
refused = says_not_found and not cited
```

with a test built from run 3's answer, which fails on the old check (`assert True is False`) and passes on the new one. Re-scored with it, `correctly_refused` across the three runs is 1.0, 0.8 and 0.8: the Core ML question was declined once in three. Kubernetes was declined every time.

The thresholds, in `evals/thresholds.json`, sit below the worst of the three runs with room for about one more unlucky case, and only on exact checks:

```json
{
  "retrieval.hybrid.recall_at_5": 0.6,
  "retrieval.hybrid.mrr": 0.4,
  "answers.cites_expected": 0.4,
  "answers.valid_citations": 0.9,
  "answers.wrongly_refused": 0.1,
  "answers.correctly_refused": 0.6
}
```

All three runs pass them. Retrieval's margin is one case (0.64 to 0.60), because retrieval doesn't vary: a drop there is always a real change. `answers.supported` has no threshold, for the reasons above.

## Trade-offs *(deep dive)*

**How many cases.** With 25 answerable cases, one case is 4 percentage points: a change that moves `cites_expected` from 0.48 to 0.52 might be one lucky answer. Hundreds of cases make small differences meaningful, at the cost of writing and checking them, and of longer runs.

**Exact checks or judges.** Exact checks are cheap, repeatable and never wrong about what they measure, but they measure proxies ("cited the right file"). Judges measure what you care about ("is it true?") and must earn trust first. Use exact checks wherever a proxy is good enough, and judges only where it isn't.

**Nondeterminism.** Atlas's chat model samples its words, so answers vary between runs. Setting the sampling temperature to 0 makes most local models nearly repeatable, but not every hosted model accepts a temperature, and real users see the varied answers anyway. Atlas measures the variation and sets thresholds below it instead.

**Strict expected files.** Many "misses" cited examples rather than the library: `examples/mnist/mnist_with_tensorboard_logger.py` for the TensorBoard question, a reasonable answer. Accepting more files per case would raise the score; it would also make it easier to pass by citing anything nearby. The strictness is a choice; write it down and keep it fixed.

**Evaluation data in the database.** The architecture once planned `eval_cases` and `eval_results` tables. Cases and grades are files instead, reviewed in pull requests like code, and each run's report is a CI artifact (decision D30).

## Common mistakes

- **Judging by a few memorable examples.** Measure on a fixed set, the same way every time.
- **Trusting a judge you haven't checked.** Grade some answers by hand and measure agreement first.
- **Only answerable cases.** A system that never declines passes them all.
- **Thresholds at last run's exact scores.** Answers vary; leave a margin, or CI fails at random.
- **Moving the target.** Changing cases, pinned commit and code in one pull request makes the scores incomparable.
- **Gating on a metric nobody trusts.** It either fails at random or passes everything.

## Check yourself

**1.** Five questions find an expected file at ranks 1, 3, none, 2, none. What are recall@5 and MRR?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
recall@5 = 3/5 = 0.6. MRR = (1 + 1/3 + 0 + 1/2 + 0) / 5 = 1.833 / 5 ≈ 0.367.
:::

**2.** The judge reports "supported 1.0". Why isn't that good news on its own?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It says nothing until the judge has been checked against a person's grades. A judge that calls everything supported also reports 1.0. Atlas's did exactly that: 4 of 10 agreement, all four on answers that really were supported.
:::

**3.** Why does the evaluation have five questions Atlas must decline?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Without them, a system that always answers (never declines) can't lose. They measure the "no citation, no claim" rule, and two of them (Kubernetes, Core ML) are the hard kind: they pass the similarity gate, so only the prompt's rule stops a made-up answer.
:::

## Exercise

Write `atlas eval-diff old.json new.json`, which compares two reports and prints each case whose hybrid retrieval rank or `cites_expected` changed, with the old and new value, then the change in each score. Test the comparison as a function on two small report dictionaries.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
def diff_reports(old: dict[str, Any], new: dict[str, Any]) -> list[str]:
    """What changed between two `atlas eval` reports: cases first, then scores."""
    lines = []
    for case_id, ranks in new["ranks"].items():
        before = old["ranks"].get(case_id, {}).get("hybrid")
        after = ranks["hybrid"]
        if before != after:
            lines.append(f"{case_id}: hybrid rank {before} -> {after}")

    old_answers = {a["case_id"]: a for a in old.get("answers", [])}
    for outcome in new.get("answers", []):
        previous = old_answers.get(outcome["case_id"])
        changed = previous is not None and previous["cites_expected"] != outcome["cites_expected"]
        if changed:
            lines.append(
                f"{outcome['case_id']}: cites_expected "
                f"{previous['cites_expected']} -> {outcome['cites_expected']}"
            )

    old_hybrid = old["scores"]["retrieval"]["hybrid"]
    for name, value in new["scores"]["retrieval"]["hybrid"].items():
        lines.append(f"retrieval.hybrid.{name}: {old_hybrid[name]} -> {value} ({value - old_hybrid[name]:+.3f})")
    old_answer_scores = old["scores"].get("answers", {})
    for name, value in new["scores"].get("answers", {}).items():
        if name in old_answer_scores:
            lines.append(f"answers.{name}: {old_answer_scores[name]} -> {value} ({value - old_answer_scores[name]:+.3f})")
    return lines
```

Two tests (a changed case and an unchanged one) pass. Run 1 against run 2:

```text
save-every-epochs: cites_expected False -> True
add-event-handler: cites_expected False -> True
time-limit: cites_expected True -> False
retrieval.hybrid.recall_at_5: 0.64 -> 0.64 (+0.000)
...
answers.cites_expected: 0.48 -> 0.52 (+0.040)
answers.correctly_refused: 1.0 -> 0.8 (-0.200)
```

"+0.04" is two cases gained and one lost: the per-case view shows how much of a difference is churn. (Between these two runs the citation rule also changed, so not all of it is luck; separating the two would need several runs of each.) The command itself is a few lines of `argparse` around the function. Not in the reference code.
:::

## Stretch

Use the retrieval part of the evaluation, which takes seconds, to test a choice from lesson 6.6: reciprocal rank fusion's constant `k = 60`. Replace `storage.reciprocal_rank_fusion` with `functools.partial(original, k=k)` (search looks the function up each time it runs, so the replacement takes effect) and score hybrid retrieval for several values:

```text
k=1     {'recall_at_5': 0.64, 'recall_at_10': 0.68, 'mrr': 0.436}
k=10    {'recall_at_5': 0.64, 'recall_at_10': 0.72, 'mrr': 0.42}
k=30    {'recall_at_5': 0.64, 'recall_at_10': 0.72, 'mrr': 0.442}
k=60    {'recall_at_5': 0.64, 'recall_at_10': 0.72, 'mrr': 0.442}
k=120   {'recall_at_5': 0.64, 'recall_at_10': 0.72, 'mrr': 0.442}
k=1000  {'recall_at_5': 0.64, 'recall_at_10': 0.72, 'mrr': 0.442}
```

From 30 up, nothing changes; very small values cost a little. The paper's 60 is safely on the flat part, and there's nothing to tune here: a result worth having, because it means time is better spent elsewhere (the 36% of questions retrieval misses). Being able to answer "does this setting matter?" in seconds is the point of having the evaluation.
